issues.claim: Pods that are not ready are not counted as available during a rolling update either, so the rollout does not progress.
issues.problem: This follows from Deployment availability semantics (maxUnavailable, minReadySeconds, rollout waiting for new Pods to become Ready). Neither linked page covers it, and the excerpts show no support. The wording 'does not progress' is also absolute, because a rollout can advance within maxUnavailable.
issues.suggestedFix: Add https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/ to links (with linkTitles in both locales), or soften the sentence to 'a rollout waits for new Pods to become Ready before it continues'.

issues.claim: In ASP.NET Core this is done with two `MapHealthChecks` calls ... `HealthCheckOptions.Predicate`.
issues.problem: The ASP.NET Core health checks API is cited in the answer, but no link covers it. MapHealthChecks, tags and HealthCheckOptions.Predicate do exist, so the claim is correct.
issues.suggestedFix: Add https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/host-and-deploy/health-checks as a third link with linkTitles in ru and en.

issues.claim: Which probe answers "may traffic be sent here right now", and which answers "should the process be restarted"?
issues.problem: The hint states the central readiness-versus-liveness distinction almost outright, so it is on the strong side.
issues.suggestedFix: Weaken it, for example: 'What does Kubernetes do with a container whose process is still alive but cannot serve requests yet, versus one that is stuck?'

issues.claim: .NET 8 and later images run the app as the non-root `app` user by default, and the SDK keeps that behaviour.
issues.problem: Official .NET 8+ images define an `app` user and APP_UID but, as far as I know, do not set it as the default USER. The SDK container tooling sets ContainerUser to `app` for .NET 8+ targets. The wording attributes the default to the images and is therefore misleading. The cited sdk-publish excerpt does not support it either.
issues.suggestedFix: Reword to: 'the .NET 8+ images include a non-root `app` user, and the SDK runs the app as that user by default for .NET 8 and later targets (override with ContainerUser)'. Cite the container configuration reference page.

issues.claim: for ASP.NET Core - aspnet, for a console app - runtime, for a self-contained app and Native AOT - runtime-deps
issues.problem: The base-image inference rules and the properties ContainerBaseImage, ContainerFamily, ContainerImageTags, ContainerPort, ContainerEnvironmentVariable and ContainerUser are not shown in either excerpt. The sdk-publish excerpt covers only publish, tarball and registry. The container-images excerpt covers image types and variants, not the SDK's choice. The Native AOT case in particular is unconfirmed.
issues.suggestedFix: Add the Microsoft Learn container publish configuration page (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/containers/publish-configuration) as a link, with linkTitles in both locales. Check the base-image wording against it, and weaken the AOT claim if it does not match.

issues.claim: Starting with the .NET 8 SDK you can build a container image of an app without a Dockerfile, for example with `dotnet publish --os linux --arch x64 -t:PublishContainer`.
issues.problem: In the early 8.0.1xx SDK band non-web projects needed EnableSdkContainerSupport, so the claim is not exactly true for every .NET 8 SDK version. The sdk-publish excerpt (a worker project) shows it working without the property in current SDKs.
issues.suggestedFix: Optionally add 'for web projects from 8.0.100 and for all projects in later SDK bands' to the explanation. Otherwise leave as is.

issues.claim: or several apps in one image
issues.problem: This is an inference from the one-project-one-image model, not a documented statement.
issues.suggestedFix: Drop it, or phrase it as 'the SDK builds one image per project'.
